text: It was raining when Rafael left the office.
He had spent ten hours in front of a screen full of numbers.
He was standing on a crowded train when he noticed a book.
Someone had left it on the seat next to him.
It's a real page-turner. I couldn't put it down.
I got hooked after the first chapter.
I was reading on the train when I missed my stop.
I hadn't read a novel in English since school.
Reading is how I switch off after work.

Every week someone comes to my desk and tells me the same thing. I used to read all the time, but now I simply haven't got the time. And I always ask: what was the last book you really enjoyed? Usually it was years ago. So here's my advice. Don't start with a classic. Start with a page-turner, something with short chapters and a good plot twist. A mystery, a thriller, a funny novel. And don't wait for a free afternoon, because it isn't coming. Read ten pages a day, on the commute, or in bed before you drift off. Within a month, most people come back and say they got hooked again.

For years, my commute was an hour each way. Two hours a day on a crowded train. I was always checking emails or reading the news on my phone, and I arrived at work already tired. Then one day a colleague gave me a detective novel. She had finished it the week before and she said, you'll love it. I didn't believe her. But I started it on the train home, and by the time I got to my station, I had read sixty pages. Since then, the train is my reading room. I've read more books in the last two years than in the ten years before.

People ask me how to write a page-turner, and I tell them there are three secrets. First, every chapter ends with a question. Not a big cliffhanger every time, just a small question in the reader's head. What was in the letter? Who had called her? Second, the characters. If the reader doesn't care about them, nothing else works. And third, the plot twist. I always plan it before I write the first page. When I write chapter one, I already know what is going to happen in chapter twelve. The reader doesn't. That's the fun part.
It was raining when he left the office.
He was reading when his phone rang.
Someone had left the book on the seat.
When I got to the station, the train had already left.
I got hooked after the first chapter.
Reading is how I switch off after work.

I hadn't read a novel in English since school.
